newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan finance reform to include foreign firms-MOF.
newsitem.headline: Japan finance reform to include foreign firms-MOF.

text.p: The planned deregulation of Japan's financial industry will encompass foreign firms as well as domestic ones, a Ministry of Finance (MOF) official told reporters on Monday.

"Foreign firms will of course be treated equally. There will be lots of business opportunities for foreign institutions in the next few years," the official said. He added that they may even have an advantage over Japanese firms at the start, as they were more used to operating in a deregulated environment.
Earlier, the Finance Ministry announced that Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto had asked the ministry to complete reform of the nation's financial system by the year 2001.
Among the deregulation plans was the abolition of the rule that only banks authorised by the Japanese government could participate in foreign exchange transactions.
The bills on foreign exchange deregulation will be submitted to the next regular session of parliament starting in January 1997, and should be enacted early in the summer of 1997, he said.
He added that the review of other related laws, such as those for securities transactions, would follow.
The deregulation was to ensure the most efficient allocation of financial resources which would encourage the inflow and outflow of funds from the Tokyo financial markets.
"We think this is the last opportunity to revitalise Tokyo's financial markets," he said.
He also said the deregulation will globalise Tokyo financial markets, which would "eventually contribute to the internationalisation of our currency".

Japan's financial reform plans also called for the promotion of entry into the banking, securities and insurance sectors, the official said, adding: "The most probable way will be by allowing holding companies. This would be a revolution."

Asked whether promoting entry into the insurance sector would affect the bilateral U.S.-Japan dispute on insurance, the MOF official said this issue had nothing to do with the deregulation policy platform, which had been hammered out by Hashimoto.
He said the prime minister would have to deal with the bilateral insurance issue but also said this would not affect major policy platforms.

Meanwhile, Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, said separately that Japan welcomes the developments that have taken place in foreign exchange markets since April 1995, and will continue to cooperate with other countries in the market.

"We welcome the developments (in foreign exchange markets) markets) since April 1995, and we continue to cooperate in the foreign exchange markets (with other countries)," he told reporters, referring to the time last year when the yen hit a record high of 79.75 yen to the dollar.
"That's our position, and it hasn't changed. The foreign exchange policy (of Japan) is unchanged," he said.
